Lazarus becomes ill (verses 1–6)

Those whom Christ loves may still become ill. Bodily afflictions can correct corruption and test the graces of believers.

Jesus did not come to protect his people from every sickness or trouble. He came to save them from sin and the wrath to come.

Nevertheless, we ought to bring sick or afflicted relatives and friends to him in prayer.

God's darkest dealings serve his glory, even when they involve sickness, loss or disappointment. When God is glorified, we may rest in his wisdom.

Jesus loved Martha, Mary and Lazarus. A family enjoying affection and peace is blessed; the happiest of all are families whose members love Jesus and are loved by him.

Even in small households, how sadly often that is not true of everyone.

God's purposes remain gracious even when help appears delayed. Deliverance for an individual, household, church or nation comes at the right time.

Jesus prepares to return to Judea (verses 7–10)

Christ never brings his people into danger without going with them.

We sometimes imagine we are defending God's cause when we are mainly defending our reputation, comfort, property or safety. We must examine our motives.

God preserves our earthly day until the work appointed to us has been finished and our testimony completed.

Someone walking in the way of duty, guided by God's word and providence, may enjoy peace and confidence.

Jesus always walked in the light of his Father's will.

Those who follow their own desires, worldly customs and merely fleshly calculations rather than God's honor stumble into temptation.

Divine light guides moral action as daylight guides our physical steps.

Jesus speaks about Lazarus's death (verses 11–16)

The promised resurrection to eternal life can make the believer's death seem like putting aside one's clothes and going to sleep.

For the Christian, death is rest after a day's labor. In one respect it is better than ordinary sleep, because it ends all earthly cares and work.

The disciples hoped Jesus would not need to return to danger.

We often wish someone else could perform the good work we have been called to do when the duty exposes us to risk.

But Lazarus's resurrection would strengthen existing believers and bring many others to faith.

Let us go to Christ. Death cannot separate us from his love or remove us beyond the reach of his call.

Like Thomas, we should encourage one another in difficult times. Our Savior's willingness to die should make us willing to die when God calls us.

Jesus reaches the grieving family (verses 17–32)

A household may fear God and enjoy his blessing and still become a house of mourning. Grace does not prevent every sorrow from visiting our homes.

When God approaches us in mercy, we should go out to meet him through faith, hope and prayer, as Martha did.

Mary remained seated in the house. Her reflective disposition had previously drawn her to Jesus' feet to hear his teaching, but in this sorrow the same inclination contributed to sadness.

We should make wise use of our natural dispositions while guarding against their particular temptations.

When we do not know precisely what to request, leave the matter in God's hands.

Jesus declared himself the Resurrection and the Life. He is resurrection's source, substance, firstfruits and cause.

The redeemed soul lives happily after death. After the resurrection, both body and soul are delivered from evil forever.

Having heard Christ's word about eternity, each of us should ask: Do I really believe this?

If we believed eternal realities as we ought, today's suffering and comfort would not dominate our feelings so completely.

Christ calls us through his word and ordinances. Those who sat at his feet to be taught in peaceful days may fall at those same feet confidently for mercy during trouble.

Jesus raises Lazarus (verses 33–46)

Jesus' distress, compassionate questions and tears revealed the tenderness of his heart.

He truly shared the grief of his friends. The Savior was a man of sorrows, acquainted with grief.

His tears give us an example of genuine compassion. But he did not praise sentimental people who weep over stories yet remain hard toward real suffering.

Instead of seeking only noisy amusements, let us make time to comfort the afflicted.

We have a High Priest who feels our weaknesses.

Before a soul receives spiritual life, prejudices and barriers often need to be removed, just as the stone was taken from Lazarus's tomb to make room for Christ's word.

If we trust Christ's promise and power, we will see God's glory.

Jesus taught us to address God as Father with both reverence and bold confidence. His public prayer showed the crowd that the Father had sent him as his beloved Son.

Jesus could have raised Lazarus silently by his own will and the Spirit's unseen life-giving power. Instead, he called aloud.

That call pictured both the gospel bringing spiritually dead sinners out of their graves and the final trumpet summoning the dead to judgment.

The grave of sin and the world is no fitting place for those Christ has made alive. They must come out.

Lazarus returned not merely to life but to health.

A sinner cannot give life to the soul, yet must use God's appointed means of grace. A believer cannot sanctify the self apart from God, yet must put aside every hindrance.

We cannot convert our relatives and friends, but we can instruct, warn and invite them.

The leaders plot against Jesus (verses 47–53)

This plot shows the desperate hostility toward God that can exist in the human heart.

Speaking prophetic words does not prove that a person has saving grace within.

The disaster people seek to escape through sin may be the very disaster their sin brings upon them.

So it is with people who oppose Christ's kingdom to protect their own interests.

Converting sinners means gathering them to Christ as their Ruler and Refuge.

He died to accomplish this, purchasing his people for himself and securing the gift of the Holy Spirit for them.

His love in dying for believers ought to unite them closely to one another.

Jesus withdraws before the Passover (verses 54–57)

Before celebrating the gospel Passover we should renew repentance and prepare seriously to meet God.

Among the Jews, some particularly devout worshipers went to Jerusalem early for purification before the feast.

Human schemes cannot change God's purposes.

While hypocrites become absorbed in forms and arguments, and worldly people pursue their plans, Jesus continues directing all things toward his glory and his people's salvation.

Verses 1-6
It is no new thing for those whom Christ loves, to be sick; bodily distempers correct the corruption, and try the graces of God's people. He came not to preserve his people from these afflictions, but to save them from their sins, and from the wrath to come; however, it behoves us to apply to Him in behalf of our friends and relatives when sick and afflicted. Let this reconcile us to the darkest dealings of Providence, that they are all for the glory of God: sickness, loss, disappointment, are so; and if God be glorified, we ought to be satisfied. Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. The families are greatly favoured in which love and peace abound; but those are most happy whom Jesus loves, and by whom he is beloved. Alas, that this should seldom be the case with every person, even in small families. God has gracious intentions, even when he seems to delay. When the work of deliverance, temporal or spiritual, public or personal, is delayed, it does but stay for the right time.
[John.11.7-John.11.10]
Verses 7-10
Christ never brings his people into any danger but he goes with them in it. We are apt to think ourselves zealous for the Lord, when really we are only zealous for our wealth, credit, ease, and safety; we have therefore need to try our principles. But our day shall be lengthened out, till our work is done, and our testimony finished. A man has comfort and satisfaction while in the way of his duty, as set forth by the word of God, and determined by the providence of God. Christ, wherever he went, walked in the day; and so shall we, if we follow his steps. If a man walks in the way of his heart, and according to the course of this world, if he consults his own carnal reasonings more than the will and glory of God, he falls into temptations and snares. He stumbles, because there is no light in him; for light in us is to our moral actions, that which light about us to our natural actions.
[John.11.11-John.11.16]
Verses 11-16
Since we are sure to rise again at the last, why should not the believing hope of that resurrection to eternal life, make it as easy for us to put off the body and die, as it is to put off our clothes and go to sleep? A true Christian, when he dies, does but sleep; he rests from the labours of the past day. Nay, herein death is better than sleep, that sleep is only a short rest, but death is the end of earthly cares and toils. The disciples thought that it was now needless for Christ to go to Lazarus, and expose himself and them. Thus we often hope that the good work we are called to do, will be done by some other hand, if there be peril in the doing of it. But when Christ raised Lazarus from the dead, many were brought to believe on him; and there was much done to make perfect the faith of those that believed. Let us go to him; death cannot separate from the love of Christ, nor put us out of the reach of his call. Like Thomas, in difficult times Christians should encourage one another. The dying of the Lord Jesus should make us willing to die whenever God calls us.
[John.11.17-John.11.32]
Verses 17-32
Here was a house where the fear of God was, and on which his blessing rested; yet it was made a house of mourning. Grace will keep sorrow from the heart, but not from the house. When God, by his grace and providence, is coming towards us in ways of mercy and comfort, we should, like Martha, go forth by faith, hope, and prayer, to meet him. When Martha went to meet Jesus, Mary sat still in the house; this temper formerly had been an advantage to her, when it put her at Christ's feet to hear his word; but in the day of affliction, the same temper disposed her to melancholy. It is our wisdom to watch against the temptations, and to make use of the advantages of our natural tempers. When we know not what in particular to ask or expect, let us refer ourselves to God; let him do as seemeth him good. To enlarge Martha's expectations, our Lord declared himself to be the Resurrection and the Life. In every sense he is the Resurrection; the source, the substance, the first-fruits, the cause of it. The redeemed soul lives after death in happiness; and after the resurrection, both body and soul are kept from all evil for ever. When we have read or heard the word of Christ, about the great things of the other world, we should put it to ourselves, Do we believe this truth? The crosses and comforts of this present time would not make such a deep impression upon us as they do, if we believed the things of eternity as we ought. When Christ our Master comes, he calls for us. He comes in his word and ordinances, and calls us to them, calls us by them, calls us to himself. Those who, in a day of peace, set themselves at Christ's feet to be taught by him, may with comfort, in a day of trouble, cast themselves at his feet, to find favour with him.
[John.11.33-John.11.46]
Verses 33-46
Christ's tender sympathy with these afflicted friends, appeared by the troubles of his spirit. In all the afflictions of believers he is afflicted. His concern for them was shown by his kind inquiry after the remains of his deceased friend. Being found in fashion as a man, he acts in the way and manner of the sons of men. It was shown by his tears. He was a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief. Tears of compassion resemble those of Christ. But Christ never approved that sensibility of which many are proud, while they weep at mere tales of distress, but are hardened to real woe. He sets us an example to withdraw from scenes of giddy mirth, that we may comfort the afflicted. And we have not a High Priest who cannot be touched with a feeling of our infirmities. It is a good step toward raising a soul to spiritual life, when the stone is taken away, when prejudices are removed, and got over, and way is made for the word to enter the heart. If we take Christ's word, and rely on his power and faithfulness, we shall see the glory of God, and be happy in the sight. Our Lord Jesus has taught us, by his own example, to call God Father, in prayer, and to draw nigh to him as children to a father, with humble reverence, yet with holy boldness. He openly made this address to God, with uplifted eyes and loud voice, that they might be convinced the Father had sent him as his beloved Son into the world. He could have raised Lazarus by the silent exertion of his power and will, and the unseen working of the Spirit of life; but he did it by a loud call. This was a figure of the gospel call, by which dead souls are brought out of the grave of sin: and of the sound of the archangel's trumpet at the last day, with which all that sleep in the dust shall be awakened, and summoned before the great tribunal. The grave of sin and this world, is no place for those whom Christ has quickened; they must come forth. Lazarus was thoroughly revived, and returned not only to life, but to health. The sinner cannot quicken his own soul, but he is to use the means of grace; the believer cannot sanctify himself, but he is to lay aside every weight and hinderance. We cannot convert our relatives and friends, but we should instruct, warn, and invite them.
[John.11.47-John.11.53]
Verses 47-53
There can hardly be a more clear discovery of the madness that is in man's heart, and of its desperate enmity against God, than what is here recorded. Words of prophecy in the mouth, are not clear evidence of a principle of grace in the heart. The calamity we seek to escape by sin, we take the most effectual course to bring upon our own heads; as those do who think by opposing Christ's kingdom, to advance their own worldly interest. The fear of the wicked shall come upon them. The conversion of souls is the gathering of them to Christ as their ruler and refuge; and he died to effect this. By dying he purchased them to himself, and the gift of the Holy Ghost for them: his love in dying for believers should unite them closely together.
[John.11.54-John.11.57]
Verses 54-57
Before our gospel passover we must renew our repentance. Thus by a voluntary purification, and by religious exercises, many, more devout than their neighbours, spent some time before the passover at Jerusalem. When we expect to meet God, we must solemnly prepare. No devices of man can alter the purposes of God: and while hypocrites amuse themselves with forms and disputes, and worldly men pursue their own plans, Jesus still orders all things for his own glory and the salvation of his people.

Mary anoints Jesus (verses 1–11)

Jesus had once corrected Martha for being distracted by too much service. She did not respond by abandoning service altogether, as people sometimes run from one extreme into another when corrected.

She continued serving, now within hearing of Christ's gracious words.

Mary expressed affection toward Jesus, who had already shown profound love to her household.

God had anointed Christ with the oil of gladness above his companions. We ought to offer him the best fragrance of our hearts' affections.

Judas concealed an ugly sin beneath a plausible concern for the poor.

We should not suppose that someone fails to serve God acceptably merely because they do not serve in our preferred way.

When the love of money rules the heart, it becomes a kind of theft within the heart.

The grace of Christ interprets godly words and deeds charitably, making the best of their imperfections and most of their goodness.

Opportunities for service must be used, especially those least likely to return.

The authorities proposed killing Lazarus, the very person Jesus had raised. Their hatred was so unreasonable that only the heart's hostility against God explains it.

The gospel's success can enrage wicked people until they behave as if they could defeat the Almighty himself.

Jesus enters Jerusalem (verses 12–19)

All four evangelists recount Jesus' triumphal entry.

His disciples did not immediately understand all that Scripture and God's providence were accomplishing.

We, too, often understand the spiritual meaning of divine events only afterward.

Understanding that Christ's kingdom is spiritual keeps us from misusing prophecies about it.

Greeks seek Jesus (verses 20–26)

Whenever we attend sacred worship, especially the gospel Passover, our deepest desire should be to see Jesus—to know him as ours, enjoy fellowship with him and receive grace from him.

The coming of Gentiles to seek him displayed the Redeemer's glory.

A grain of wheat bears no harvest unless it falls into the ground.

Christ could have remained in heavenly glory without becoming human. Even after taking human nature, he might have entered heaven by his own perfect righteousness without suffering or death.

But then no human sinner could have been saved.

Every soul saved before Christ's crucifixion, and every soul saved afterward, depends upon the death of this grain of wheat.

Let us ask whether Christ lives within us as our hope of glory. May he loosen our attachment to trivial concerns, enabling us to serve willingly and follow his holy example.

A heavenly voice testifies to Jesus (verses 27–33)

Our sins brought distress to Christ's soul when he undertook to redeem us and offer his soul for our sins.

He was willing to suffer, yet still prayed to be delivered from suffering.

Praying against trouble can coexist with patient submission to God's will.

Christ humbled himself to satisfy the honor of God offended through human sin.

The Father had already declared Jesus his beloved Son at his baptism and transfiguration. Now a voice again confirmed that God's name had been glorified and would be glorified.

By the merit of his death Christ reconciles sinners to God, breaks death's dominion and casts Satan down as a destroyer.

Through the teaching of his cross, he breaks sin's power and drives Satan out as a deceiver.

Souls once far from Christ come to love and trust him. Ascending to heaven, Jesus draws their hearts toward himself.

There is power in Christ's death to draw sinners to him.

The gospel exalts free grace and commands duty. We must embrace both sincerely rather than separate them.

Jesus urges the people to walk in the light (verses 34–36)

The listeners misunderstood Scripture because they overlooked the prophecies about the Messiah's suffering and death.

Jesus told them the light would remain among them only a little longer. They should believe it and walk in it before darkness overtook them.

Without faith, people fail to recognize the saving significance of Jesus lifted upon the cross and cannot experience its power as revealed by the Holy Spirit.

They invent countless objections to justify unbelief.

Many refuse to believe (verses 37–43)

Conversion begins as sinners see the reality of divine things.

They learn something of God's truth and turn from sin to Christ as their happiness and their portion.

God heals them: justifying and sanctifying them, forgiving sins like open wounds and mortifying corrupt desires like hidden diseases.

But worldly approval can smother even serious convictions.

A desire for human praise can make people hypocrites when religion is fashionable and earns respect.

The same desire can make them apostates when religion is despised and threatens their reputation.

Jesus gives his final public appeal (verses 44–50)

Jesus publicly taught that faith in him is also faith in the Father who sent him.

In Christ we see the Father's glory and learn to obey, love and trust the Father.

By continually looking to Jesus, the light of the world, we are increasingly freed from the darkness of ignorance, error, sin and misery.

God our Savior's command is everlasting life.

Yet the same divine word will confirm the condemnation of those who reject or neglect it.

Verses 1-11
Christ had formerly blamed Martha for being troubled with much serving. But she did not leave off serving, as some, who when found fault with for going too far in one way, peevishly run too far another way; she still served, but within hearing of Christ's gracious words. Mary gave a token of love to Christ, who had given real tokens of his love to her and her family. God's Anointed should be our Anointed. Has God poured on him the oil of gladness above his fellows, let us pour on him the ointment of our best affections. In Judas a foul sin is gilded over with a plausible pretence. We must not think that those do no acceptable service, who do it not in our way. The reigning love of money is heart-theft. The grace of Christ puts kind comments on pious words and actions, makes the best of what is amiss, and the most of what is good. Opportunities are to be improved; and those first and most vigorously, which are likely to be the shortest. To consult to hinder the further effect of the miracle, by putting Lazarus to death, is such wickedness, malice, and folly, as cannot be explained, except by the desperate enmity of the human heart against God. They resolved that the man should die whom the Lord had raised to life. The success of the gospel often makes wicked men so angry, that they speak and act as if they hoped to obtain a victory over the Almighty himself.
[John.12.12-John.12.19]
Verses 12-19
Christ's riding in triumph to Jerusalem is recorded by all the evangelists. Many excellent things, both in the word and providence of God, disciples do not understand at their first acquaintance with the things of God. The right understanding of spiritual nature of Christ's kingdom, prevents our misapplying the Scriptures which speak of it.
[John.12.20-John.12.26]
Verses 20-26
In attendance upon holy ordinances, particularly the gospel passover, the great desire of our souls should be to see Jesus; to see him as ours, to keep up communion with him, and derive grace from him. The calling of the Gentiles magnified the Redeemer. A corn of wheat yields no increase unless it is cast into the ground. Thus Christ might have possessed his heavenly glory alone, without becoming man. Or, after he had taken man's nature, he might have entered heaven alone, by his own perfect righteousness, without suffering or death; but then no sinner of the human race could have been saved. The salvation of souls hitherto, and henceforward to the end of time, is owing to the dying of this Corn of wheat. Let us search whether Christ be in us the hope of glory; let us beg him to make us indifferent to the trifling concerns of this life, that we may serve the Lord Jesus with a willing mind, and follow his holy example.
[John.12.27-John.12.33]
Verses 27-33
The sin of our souls was the troubled of Christ's soul, when he undertook to redeem and save us, and to make his soul an offering for our sin. Christ was willing to suffer, yet prayed to be saved from suffering. Prayer against trouble may well agree with patience under it, and submission to the will of God in it. Our Lord Jesus undertook to satisfy God's injured honour, and he did it by humbling himself. The voice of the Father from heaven, which had declared him to be his beloved Son, at his baptism, and when he was transfigured, was heard proclaiming that He had both glorified his name, and would glorify it. Christ, reconciling the world to God by the merit of his death, broke the power of death, and cast out Satan as a destroyer. Christ, bringing the world to God by the doctrine of his cross, broke the power of sin, and cast out Satan as a deceiver. The soul that was at a distance from Christ, is brought to love him and trust him. Jesus was now going to heaven, and he would draw men's hearts to him thither. There is power in the death of Christ to draw souls to him. We have heard from the gospel that which exalts free grace, and we have heard also that which enjoins duty; we must from the heart embrace both, and not separate them.
[John.12.34-John.12.36]
Verses 34-36
The people drew false notions from the Scriptures, because they overlooked the prophecies that spoke of Christ's sufferings and death. Our Lord warned them that the light would not long continue with them, and exhorted them to walk in it, before the darkness overtook them. Those who would walk in the light must believe in it, and follow Christ's directions. But those who have not faith, cannot behold what is set forth in Jesus, lifted up on the cross, and must be strangers to its influence as made known by the Holy Spirit; they find a thousand objections to excuse their unbelief.
[John.12.37-John.12.43]
Verses 37-43
Observe the method of conversion implied here. Sinners are brought to see the reality of Divine things, and to have some knowledge of them. To be converted, and truly turned from sin to Christ, as their Happiness and Portion. God will heal them, will justify and sanctify them; will pardon their sins, which are as bleeding wounds, and mortify their corruptions, which are as lurking diseases. See the power of the world in smothering convictions, from regard to the applause or censure of men. Love of the praise of men, as a by-end in that which is good, will make a man a hypocrite when religion is in fashion, and credit is to be got by it; and love of the praise of men, as a base principle in that which is evil, will make a man an apostate, when religion is in disgrace, and credit is to be lost for it.
[John.12.44-John.12.50]
Verses 44-50
Our Lord publicly proclaimed, that every one who believed on him, as his true disciple, did not believe on him only, but on the Father who sent him. Beholding in Jesus the glory of the Father, we learn to obey, love, and trust in him. By daily looking to Him, who came a Light into the world, we are more and more freed from the darkness of ignorance, error, sin, and misery; we learn that the command of God our Saviour is everlasting life. But the same word will seal the condemnation of all who despise it, or neglect it.

Jesus washes his disciples' feet (verses 1–17)

The Lord Jesus has people who belong to him. He purchased them at great cost, set them apart and called them to devote themselves to him.

Those he loves, he loves to the end. Nothing can separate a true believer from Christ's love.

Because we do not know when our last hour will arrive, we must never neglect the constant preparation it requires.

We cannot fully understand how the devil enters human hearts. Yet some sins are so dreadful, with so little ordinary enticement from the world or flesh, that Henry sees Satan's direct influence in them.

Jesus washed his disciples' feet to teach us that no task should be considered beneath us if it glorifies God and helps our fellow believers. We must undertake our duties and remove whatever hinders us.

The washing pictured the cleansing of souls from sin's pollution.

The disciples did not yet know why Jesus did everything he did. Events that initially seem painful may later reveal his kindness.

Rejecting the gospel because its gifts seem too generous to be true is unbelief, not humility.

Only those spiritually washed by Christ have a share in him. He both justifies and sanctifies everyone whom he saves.

Peter went beyond submission and asked to be washed completely. Genuine desire for holiness seeks purity in every faculty and part of the person.

Believers receive their fundamental cleansing when they receive Christ as Savior. Yet those already justified must attend to daily cleansing, confessing fresh guilt and resisting whatever might defile them.

Yesterday's pardon should equip us to withstand today's temptation.

Nor should we be surprised if a hypocrite among Christ's professed followers is exposed.

The Lord also taught mutual service. We must accept help from one another as well as give it.

How unworthy it is to lord over fellow believers when our Master himself served them! His love continues after reconciling people who had once been his enemies.

Jesus foretells the betrayal (verses 18–30)

Jesus had often spoken about his approaching suffering and death, but the betrayal by Judas caused him particular grief.

The sins of those professing Christ's name grieve him. We should not restrict this warning to Judas.

Think of the unbeliever who studies Scripture only to undermine its authority, the hypocrite who professes Scripture while refusing to obey it, and the apostate who abandons Christ for a worthless advantage.

Human beings eat the bread supplied by divine Providence and then raise their heel against their generous Provider.

Judas departed as though tired of Jesus and his apostles.

Those who practice evil love darkness rather than light.

Jesus commands the disciples to love one another (verses 31–38)
The glory of the cross and the new command (verses 31–35)

Jesus had displayed glory through many miracles, yet spoke of his coming suffering as bringing greater glory than any miracle of his humbled ministry.

Through the cross, satisfaction was made for the wrong done to God's honor by human sin.

The disciples could not yet follow him to heavenly happiness. Believers will follow later, but must now wait and fulfill his work.

Jesus gave them a new commandment: they were to love one another for his sake and by his example, seeking each other's good and advancing the gospel together, like one body animated by one spirit.

Strangely, this command remains new to many professing believers. People attend to almost any other teaching of Christ before this one.

If Christians fail to love one another, they give others reason to doubt the sincerity of their discipleship.

Peter's confidence and Christ's warning (verses 36–38)

Peter passed over Jesus' command to love and questioned him about matters Jesus had deliberately kept hidden.

We often want to learn the secret things that belong to God rather than the revealed duties that belong to us and our children.

We prefer satisfying curiosity to directing our consciences, or debating heavenly mysteries to learning how to reach heaven.

Plain and helpful truth is often abandoned while doubtful disputes become endless quarrels.

We dislike being told we cannot do something, forgetting that without Christ we can do nothing.

Jesus knows us better than we know ourselves. He has many ways to reveal the condition of those he loves and to hide pride from them.

May we preserve the unity of the Spirit through peace, love one another sincerely and walk humbly with our God.

Verses 1-17
Our Lord Jesus has a people in the world that are his own; he has purchased them, and paid dear for them, and he has set them apart for himself; they devote themselves to him as a peculiar people. Those whom Christ loves, he loves to the end. Nothing can separate a true believer from the love of Christ. We know not when our hour will come, therefore what we have to do in constant preparation for it, ought never to be undone. What way of access the devil has to men's hearts we cannot tell. But some sins are so exceedingly sinful, and there is so little temptation to them from the world and the flesh, that it is plain they are directly from Satan. Jesus washed his disciples' feet, that he might teach us to think nothing below us, wherein we may promote God's glory, and the good of our brethren. We must address ourselves to duty, and must lay aside every thing that would hinder us in what we have to do. Christ washed his disciples' feet, that he might signify to them the value of spiritual washing, and the cleansing of the soul from the pollutions of sin. Our Lord Jesus does many things of which even his own disciples do not for the present know the meaning, but they shall know afterward. We see in the end what was the kindness from events which seemed most cross. Jesus Christ is the true Vine.

A vine should produce grapes, and Christians should display Christian character and a life that honors God and benefits others.

Branches that bear no fruit are removed. But even fruitful branches must be pruned.

The best believers retain mistaken ideas, passions and dispositions that need correcting.

People who do not remain in him may flourish outwardly for a time in religious profession but finally achieve nothing.

A hypocrite's joy lasts briefly. Those remaining in Christ's love enjoy a lasting feast.

They show love for him by keeping his commandments.

But unless the same divine power that first poured Christ's love into our hearts continued to preserve it, we could not remain in that love for long.

The love we receive from Christ must direct our love toward one another.

Jesus foretells persecution (verses 1–6)

Jesus warned his disciples about coming trouble so they would not be caught unprepared and overwhelmed by fear.

People genuinely opposed to God's service may pretend to be zealously serving him.

Religious language does not make wicked deeds righteous. Evil remains evil even when committed in God's name.

As Christ looked to the fulfillment of Scripture during his suffering, so should his followers during theirs.

Jesus had not previously needed to speak so fully about the Spirit's coming because he was still present to teach, guide and comfort the disciples.

When we suffer, asking where the trouble came from may leave us confused; asking where God is leading it can satisfy us, because his purpose is our good.

Sorrowful Christians often dwell on the cloud's dark side and refuse to hear the voice of joy.

The disciples' excessive attachment to this present life intensified their sadness.

Nothing so obstructs joy in God as love of the world and the worldly grief it produces.

Christ's departure was necessary for the Comforter to come.

The Spirit's coming followed Christ's death, which his departure would accomplish.

Jesus' bodily presence was limited to one place at a time, but his Spirit is present wherever his people gather in his name, at every time and place.

The Spirit first convicts, and then comforts.

Conviction is his work, and only he can accomplish it effectively.

He convinces sinners of sin in its many aspects: its reality, guilt, folly, pollution, source in fallen human nature and final consequence in death.

He shows the whole world guilty before God.

The Spirit also convicts concerning righteousness.

Jesus of Nazareth is the righteous Christ. His righteousness is made available to believers for justification and salvation.

The Spirit shows sinners where righteousness may be found and how they can be accepted before God.

Christ's ascension demonstrates that the ransom has been accepted and the saving righteousness completed.

The Spirit convicts concerning judgment.

The ruler of this world has been judged. When Satan's power is broken, believers can be confident that no rival power can overcome Christ.

This also directs our thoughts toward the final day of judgment.

The Spirit's coming was therefore an immeasurable benefit to the disciples.

He is not merely a guide pointing to the way but a companion helping them walk in it.

Being led into truth means more than carrying correct ideas in the mind.

It means tasting the goodness and knowing the power of truth in the heart.

He will make every profitable truth known and reveal what is to come.

The Spirit's gifts and graces, the apostles' preaching and writing, their languages and miracles—all were intended to glorify Christ.

Each of us should ask whether the Spirit has begun a good work within us.

Unless we recognize our guilt and danger, we will not understand the greatness of Christ's salvation.

The more we pray for and depend on the Spirit, the more clearly we will see the Redeemer and the more deeply we will love him.

Grief will become joy (verses 16–22)

We should remember how quickly our opportunities for grace can pass and use them faithfully.

The disciples' sorrow would soon give way to joy, like a mother's pain replaced by happiness at the sight of her newborn child.

The Holy Spirit would comfort them, and neither people nor demons, suffering nor death, could permanently steal their joy.

Believers' sorrow or gladness is closely connected with their sense of Christ's presence and favor.

The ungodly are approaching sorrow that nothing can relieve.

Believers, however, inherit joy that no one can take away.

Where is the happiness now of those who murdered the Lord, compared with the lasting joy of his friends?

Asking something of the Father acknowledges spiritual need, desires spiritual blessings and recognizes that only God can supply them.

Praying in Christ's name acknowledges our unworthiness and depends entirely on Christ as the Lord our Righteousness.

After his resurrection he intended to speak more plainly about the Father and access to him through his intercession.

Jesus repeatedly commanded prayer in his name because his mediation teaches us our sinfulness and the value and power of his atoning death, by which we approach God.

We may address the Father in Christ's name or address the Son as God in human nature who reconciles sinners to himself.

These approaches belong together because the Father and the Son are one.

Jesus came from the Father as God revealed in human nature, and he would return to the Father and be received into glory.

The disciples understood more and their faith increased.

The divine nature never abandoned Christ's human nature during his sufferings.

It supported him, giving his suffering strength and worth.

When God is graciously present with us, we can be content even when everyone else deserts us.

True peace is found in Christ alone.

Through him we have peace with God, and therefore peace within our hearts.

Christ has already conquered the world.

Yet believers must remain watchful, for those who think they stand can still fall.

We do not know how we would behave under severe temptation.
